title: Preparation of standard sodium carbonate solution
objective: Calculate the mass of anhydrous Na2CO3 needed for a solution of stated normality and volume
Weigh, transfer completely and make up to the mark in a volumetric flask
Explain why anhydrous (not hydrated) sodium carbonate is used as the primary standard here
State the normality relation for a base that accepts two protons

theory.statement: Anhydrous sodium carbonate is a widely used primary standard for standardising acids, because it can be obtained pure and of exactly known, stable composition (unlike the hydrated form, which can lose or gain water of crystallisation on standing).
theory.derivationNote: Na2CO3 reacts with acid in two proton-accepting steps (to HCO3-, then to H2CO3/CO2+H2O), so its equivalent mass for full neutralisation is half its molar mass: 106.0/2 = 53.0. A 250 mL flask of 0.1 N sodium carbonate therefore needs mass = 0.1 × 53.0 × 0.250 ≈ 1.325 g.
keyEquations: Normality N = M × 2 (Na2CO3 accepts two protons)

safety: Sodium carbonate dust is a mild irritant — avoid inhaling while weighing.
sourcesOfError: Using the hydrated (washing soda) form by mistake gives a completely wrong concentration, since its molar mass includes ten water molecules.
Incomplete transfer or overshooting the mark, as with any standard solution.

viva.question: Why is anhydrous, not hydrated, sodium carbonate used here?
viva.expectedConcept: The hydrated form (washing soda, Na2CO3·10H2O) can lose water of crystallisation on standing in dry air, so its exact composition — and hence the mass needed for a given concentration — is not reliably known. The anhydrous form has a fixed, known molar mass.
viva.answerLogic: Variable water content spoils the 'exactly known mass' requirement.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming any form of sodium carbonate works equally well.

viva.question: Why does sodium carbonate have an equivalent mass of half its molar mass here?
viva.expectedConcept: The carbonate ion accepts two protons in its full neutralisation by a strong acid (CO3^2- + 2H+ → H2O + CO2), so each mole supplies two 'equivalents', giving equivalent mass = molar mass/2.
viva.answerLogic: Two-proton acceptance halves the equivalent mass.
viva.commonMisconception: Using the molar mass directly as if it were monoacidic.

viva.question: This standard solution is later titrated against hydrochloric acid using methyl orange. Why not phenolphthalein?
viva.expectedConcept: Phenolphthalein changes colour around pH 8-10, at the bicarbonate stage of the reaction, ending the titration a full equivalence early. Methyl orange changes near pH 3-4, close to the true final equivalence point where all the carbonate has been converted to CO2 and water.
viva.answerLogic: Indicator range must match the true equivalence pH, not an intermediate stage.
viva.commonMisconception: Choosing an indicator by habit rather than by the equivalence pH of this specific reaction.

preLab.question: The equivalent mass of Na2CO3 (molar mass 106) as a base is:
preLab.feedback: It accepts two protons on complete neutralisation, so equivalent mass = 106/2 = 53.
